coherence.reasons: Both follow a clean hierarchy from governing thought to sections to slide evidence, and both reach the same Pro-plan answer. Y sets out one key question with five sub-questions, and each section answers one of them; the summary lines match the section titles and the supporting numbers. X is tight too, but has two small seams. Its second summary point sizes the prize on the add-on ($2.5M) while the governing thought plans on Pro ($2.9M). Its closing $2.4M net figure adds win-back at its ceiling while describing the sum as 'both risks counted at their ceiling', which blurs the logic. Y's 'worth the delay, narrowly' line is consistent with its own break-even analysis.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the answer key's preferred recommendation: Pro tier with a usage allowance, sized on the paywall test, with the mobile restart date locked. Y weighs more alternatives and weighs them better. It tests the add-on, Pro and free-in-Core against the NRR and margin targets (free-in-Core falls to 71.9%; a capped free tier holds 75% but earns nothing). It also compares Copilot-first with mobile-first directly, giving a break-even: mobile-first wins if the rewrite would prevent more than about 29% of mobile churn in its first two quarters. It admits the call is narrow. Y also notes that the Pro NRR lift is one-off and that new-logo wins do not count in NRR, both of which matter for the 105% objective. X quantifies the mobile delay ($1.1M ceiling) and sets sensible conditions, but never treats mobile-first as an option. Its single net figure of $2.4M makes the trade-off look more settled than it is.

evidence.reasons: The arithmetic I checked in both documents reproduces: $2.45M against $8M, inference of $32.4 / $61.2 / $130.5 per account, 109 wins worth about $0.6M, Pro at $2.89M, the 26% NRR threshold and the $1.1M mobile ceiling. Both reject the VP Sales memo for the right reasons and flag volunteer bias, survey non-response and the Routewise discount. X's Pro inference cost ($32.4 per account, about 56% tier margin) matches the answer key. Y normalises per seat ($4 per seat, about a third of the premium), which is a more optimistic but stated assumption, and it stress-tests it at paywall-buyer use (63% of premium, 75.05% company margin). Y adds valid points X lacks: renewal was measured while Copilot was free, the win-rate periods differ in length, 17 of 120 is a small sample, and the add-on leaves under $1M of gross profit after costs. X's weak spots are the net figure that adds upside at its ceiling and leaves out engineering and run costs, the unsupported 'so does use' claim, and a more causal slide title on the win-rate fall. Y's 'near-certain' revenue gain is a mild overclaim given that the 33% migration rate comes from a different tier.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CPO's hypothesis as the answer key expects: keep the launch, drop the $149 add-on and replace the $8M survey figure with about $2.5M from the paywall test. Both explain the gap through stated versus revealed preference plus the 6% response rate and the size skew. Both also take down the VP Sales claim. Y goes a little further: it recomputes the plan to $8.06M, shows the add-on leaves under $1M of gross profit after inference and platform costs, and shows the add-on has almost no headroom against the NRR target. It also takes the Head of Customer Success's mobile concern seriously with an explicit mobile-first comparison. X's revision is correct and clear but less developed.

overall.reasons: The two documents give the same recommendation on essentially the same correct core numbers, so the difference is in how well they prepare the executive team for the hard parts of the decision. Y does this better. It compares Copilot-first with mobile-first and gives a break-even condition. It shows why free-in-Core fails the margin floor, and it warns that the Pro NRR lift is one-off. It also supplies payback, sensitivity cases, risk owners and a scorecard. X is more concise and matches the answer key's Pro-margin figure more closely, and its next steps (separate AI from the discount in win-loss data, test on non-volunteers) are good. But its single net $2.4M figure overstates how settled the mobile trade-off is, and it never weighs delaying Copilot as an option.
